source.value: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, the velocity is given by $v(x)=(1+x)\,m/s.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$

authoring.value:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041958/assets/0dd98b517e2ed800f12a3672d2d6f45021f7f502cfe98c1e9308e52c05ab5f38.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x/2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{e}^{x/2}+C.
$$

Now, since  $v=\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{5})^{2} & =2{e}^{0/2}+C \\ \frac{5}{2} & =2+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{x/2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{x/2}+1 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4{e}^{1/2}+1} \\ v & =\sqrt{4\sqrt{e}+1} \\  & ≈2.8\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

authoring.value:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041958/assets/634a0680d0f159006c524b8d0eb466b2c99b0f9b5a46cf38b7cd689c9d8d6fb2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $6\sqrt[3]{x+1}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=6\sqrt[3]{x+1}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=6\sqrt[3]{x+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 6\sqrt[3]{x+1}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{9(x+1)^{4/3}}{2}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=12\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=7\,\text{m}$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{9(x+1)^{4/3}}{2}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(12)^{2} & =\frac{9(7+1)^{4/3}}{2}+K \\ 72 & =72+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{9(x+1)^{4/3}}{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =9(x+1)^{4/3} \\ v & =\pm 3(x+1)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=3(x+1)^{2/3}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3(x+1)^{2/3}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3(x+1)^{2/3} \\ \frac{1}{3(x+1)^{2/3}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{3(x+1)^{2/3}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{3(x+1)^{2/3}}\text{d}x & =\int \text{d}t \\ \sqrt[3]{x+1} & =t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=7$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
\sqrt[3]{x+1}=t+2.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{x+1} & =t+2 \\ x+1 & =(t+2)^{3} \\ x & =(t+2)^{3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$
